props.title: The Year My Parents Went on Vacation
props.initialSlug: A boy finds identity during Brazil's 1970 Cup fever

sections.content: **The Year My Parents Went on Vacation** (2006) masterfully captures Brazil's political turmoil through a child's eyes, joining other powerful films about childhood during dictatorships like **Pan's Labyrinth** (2006) and **Machuca** (2004). Director Cao Hamburger crafts an intimate portrait of 12-year-old Mauro, suddenly left in São Paulo's Jewish quarter when his leftist parents go "on vacation" - a euphemism for fleeing the military regime. The film's genius lies in how it balances Brazil's 1970 World Cup fever with the undercurrent of political repression, similar to how **Roma** (2018) used personal story to illuminate broader social upheaval.

sections.content: The film's portrayal of Brazil's Jewish community adds rich cultural texture, reminiscent of how **Avalon** (1990) depicted Baltimore's Jewish immigrants or **Crossing Delancey** (1988) captured New York's Lower East Side. Hamburger's attention to period detail - from the yellow-green Brazilian soccer jerseys to the vintage TV broadcasts - creates an authentic time capsule of 1970 Brazil, when soccer glory temporarily masked political oppression. The community's embrace of Mauro mirrors similar themes in **Au Revoir Les Enfants** (1987), where religious and cultural boundaries blur in times of crisis.

The film's greatest achievement is maintaining Mauro's child perspective while subtly revealing the adult world's dangers. This delicate balance recalls **Empire of the Sun** (1987) and **Hope and Glory** (1987), where young protagonists navigate war's chaos with a mix of innocence and growing awareness. The World Cup celebrations provide a brilliant metaphor for national identity and collective escape, similar to how **Forbidden Games** (1952) used children's play to process trauma. sections.content: Brazilian cinema has excelled at examining dictatorship through young characters, from **Pixote** (1981) to **The Official Story** (1985). These films share a powerful tradition with other Latin American works like **Bad Hair** (2013) and **Tigers Are Not Afraid** (2017), using children's perspectives to critique societal upheaval. Hamburger's film stands out for its warmth and humanity, finding moments of joy amid political darkness.
